scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

Remember, prioritize tasks based on your schedule and energy levels. Don't hesitate to ask for help if you need it, and enjoy the festive spirit of Diwali!

prediction.raw: I can't provide a definitive answer on whether you would be an asshole or not. However, I can offer some insights and concerns about your approach. Forcing your son to participate in a sport or extracurricular activity without his consent or genuine interest may not be the most effective or healthy approach. Here's why: 1. **Lack of autonomy**: Forcing your son to participate in an activity without his input or consent may undermine his sense of autonomy and self-determination. This could lead to resentment and a negative association with the activity. 2. **Potential for burnout**: Coercing your son into a sport or activity he's not interested in may lead to burnout, decreased motivation, and a negative experience. 3. **Missed opportunity for intrinsic motivation**: By forcing your son to participate, you may be missing an opportunity to help him develop intrinsic motivation and a genuine interest in the activity. 4. **Impact on relationship**: Forcing your son to participate in an activity he doesn't want to do may damage your relationship with him, especially if he feels you're not respecting his boundaries or interests. Instead of forcing your son to participate, consider the following approaches: 1. **Have an open conversation**: Talk to your son about your concerns and listen to his perspective. Understand his interests and values, and explore ways to help him develop a growth mindset and a sense of purpose. 2. **Encourage exploration**: Support your son in exploring different activities and interests. This can help him discover what he enjoys and what he's good at. 3. **Set clear expectations and boundaries**: Establish clear expectations and boundaries for your son's behavior, such as completing his homework, helping with household chores, and taking care of his personal hygiene. 4. **Model positive behavior**: Demonstrate positive behavior yourself, such as being active, trying new things, and taking care of your own well-being. This can inspire your son to adopt similar habits. 5. **Seek professional help**: If your son's behavior persists and is causing concern, consider seeking help from a therapist or counselor who can work with you and your son to develop strategies for improving his behavior and motivation. Remember, every child is unique, and what works for one child may not work for another. By taking a more collaborative and supportive approach, you may be able to help your son develop a more positive and productive mindset.
